label: Shemu'el Aleph (1 Samuel) — Part 1 — Chapters 1–10
summary_plain: Chanah prays at Shiloh for a son and vows to give him to YHWH. Shemu'el is born and dedicated to the service of YHWH at the Mishkan. The boy Shemu'el hears YHWH calling his name at night. The Philistines capture the Ark — Eli's sons Chofni and Pinchas are killed. The Ark is returned. The people demand a king like the nations. YHWH tells Shemu'el: they have not rejected you — they have rejected me from being king over them. Sha'ul son of Kish from Binyamin is anointed as the first king.
summary_scholarly: The ACR reads from the Dead Sea Scrolls witnesses (4QSam-a, 4QSam-b, 4QSam-c) and the Orit Ge'ez. The DSS Samuel manuscripts are among the most significant textual finds at Qumran — 4QSam-a preserves readings that differ substantially from the Masoretic and often agree with the Septuagint, confirming the Masoretic as a later editorial tradition. The demand for a king (ch 8) is YHWH's direct assessment: they have rejected YHWH as king. Monarchy is presented as a concession to human weakness, not YHWH's original design.

key_terms.definition: The mother of Shemu'el, barren and deeply distressed. She prays silently at Shilo with such intensity that Eli the priest thinks she is drunk. She vows: 'YHWH of Hosts, if you will look on the affliction of your servant and give her a son, I will give him to YHWH all the days of his life.' YHWH hears; Shemu'el is born; she gives him to Eli at Shilo.

1 Shemu'el 2: Khannah's prayer of thanksgiving — the original. It opens: 'My heart exults in YHWH; my strength is lifted in YHWH.' It announces: YHWH kills and makes alive, casts down and raises up, lifts the poor from the dust. The prayer of Miryam of the NT literary construct borrows its structure directly from this earlier prayer by Khannah — Khannah is the source.

Eli was the high priest at Shilo. His sons Khofni and Pinkhas treated the offerings of YHWH with contempt — taking meat by force before it was offered, sleeping with women who served at the Tent door. Eli rebuked them but did not remove them. YHWH sent a man of YHWH and then Shemu'el to announce judgment: Eli's house would be cut off.

1 Shemu'el 3: the boy Shemu'el hears his name called at night three times and runs to Eli each time, thinking it was Eli calling. After the third time, Eli understands: 'Go lie down, and if he calls you, say: Speak, YHWH, for your servant is listening.' The word the YHWH gives is judgment against Eli's house — Shemu'el must deliver it to the man who raised him.

1 Shemu'el 4: Yisra'el brings the Ark of the Covenant to battle against the Philistines, thinking its presence guarantees victory. The Philistines win, Khofni and Pinkhas are killed, the Ark is captured. Eli falls off his seat at the news and breaks his neck. His daughter-in-law, dying in childbirth, names the child Ikavod — 'the glory has departed from Yisra'el.'

'Where is the glory?' or 'No glory' — the name given by Eli's dying daughter-in-law when she hears the Ark is captured and her husband Pinkhas is dead. 'The glory has departed from Yisra'el.' The name marks the low point of Eli's era: the covenant presence (the Ark) is in Philistine hands, the priestly family is destroyed, and a dying woman names the moment for all of Yisra'el.

1 Shemu'el 5-6: the Philistines place the Ark in Dagon's temple and find their statue fallen before it twice — the second time shattered at the threshold. YHWH strikes the Philistine cities with plagues. After seven months, they send the Ark back on a cart pulled by nursing cows with their calves shut away — if the cows go toward Bet-Shemesh without their calves, it was YHWH's hand.

The first king of Yisra'el, from the tribe of Binyamin. He is introduced while searching for his father's lost donkeys and encounters Shemu'el, who anoints him in private. At the public selection at Mitspah by lot, Sha'ul is chosen but found hiding among the baggage. His physical description: head and shoulders taller than any in Yisra'el.

1 Shemu'el 8: when the elders ask Shemu'el for a king, YHWH tells him: 'They have not rejected you; they have rejected me from being king over them.' Shemu'el warns the people exactly what a king will do — take their sons for his army, their daughters for his household, their fields and vineyards and flocks. 'You will cry out because of your king, but YHWH will not answer you in that day.'

1 Shemu'el 7: Shemu'el assembles Yisra'el at Mitspah, they confess sin, fast and pour water before YHWH. The Philistines attack; YHWH thunders over them and they are thrown into confusion. After the victory Shemu'el sets up a stone named 'Ebenezer' — 'Stone of Help' — saying: 'Till now YHWH has helped us.' Covenant return produces covenant victory.

faq.question: Why is Khannah's prayer theologically significant?
faq.answer: Khannah's prayer is the first great covenant hymn in the narrative books — a psalm before Tehillim. It opens with personal gratitude but immediately becomes universal covenant theology: YHWH kills and makes alive, casts down and raises up, lifts the poor from the dust, the needy from the ash heap, to seat them with princes. The prayer is not merely about a barren woman receiving a son; it is a declaration that YHWH's power works through reversals — the unexpected, the marginalized, the apparently defeated. This prayer will echo through Yisra'el's covenant history (and is the source from which the NT construct's 'Magnificat' drew).

faq.question: What does Shemu'el's call reveal about YHWH's pattern of choosing spokespersons?
faq.answer: Shemu'el is a child sleeping in the Temple when YHWH first calls him. He does not know what a divine call sounds or feels like. He needs Eli — the man whose house he is called to judge — to teach him how to respond. YHWH's pattern is consistent: the called person is the last to understand the calling. Mosheh argued at the burning bush; Gid'on hid in a winepress; Shemu'el ran to the wrong person three times. The commissioning of a spokesperson always begins in the gap between YHWH's choice and the human's self-understanding. YHWH does not wait for the person to feel ready.

faq.question: What does the capture of the Ark teach about covenant presumption?
faq.answer: Yisra'el brought the Ark to battle thinking its physical presence guaranteed victory. The Philistines were terrified when they heard it arrived — 'YHWH has come into the camp.' But Yisra'el lost anyway. YHWH is not a battle talisman carried for automatic victory. His presence at the Ark does not compel him to protect an army whose priests were sinning (Khofni and Pinkhas were there). Covenant is not mechanical — the right object in the right place does not substitute for covenant fidelity. The Ark's capture is YHWH refusing to protect his own symbol from an enemy in order to judge his own unfaithful people.

faq.question: What is the significance of the Dagon collapse before the Ark?
faq.answer: The Philistines placed the Ark in Dagon's temple as war tribute — the captured deity of the defeated people placed before the victor's deity. Instead, Dagon fell prostrate before the Ark twice. The second time his head and hands broke off on the threshold — the threshold where worshippers' feet crossed. The priests avoided stepping on the threshold afterward. YHWH did not need Yisra'el's army to demonstrate his superiority over Dagon; he demonstrated it alone, in the enemy's own temple, at night. The Ark's presence was not defeated — it was the Philistines' punishment. The captured deity was actually the captor.

faq.question: How does YHWH's speech about the king in 1 Shemu'el 8 frame the entire monarchy?
faq.answer: YHWH's response to the king demand is explicit: 'They have rejected me from being king over them.' The monarchy is granted as a concession, not a blessing. YHWH then instructs Shemu'el to tell the people exactly what a king will do — take their sons for chariots and horsemen, their daughters for perfumers and cooks, their fields and vineyards, their flocks. 'You will be his slaves.' This is not prophecy — it is structural description of what monarchy means. The people insist anyway: 'We will have a king over us that we may be like all the nations.' The desire to be like the nations is itself the problem — Yisra'el's covenant identity is specifically different from the nations. YHWH grants the demand as a judgment they will live with.

faq.question: Who was Khannah's prayer addressed to and why does that matter?
faq.answer: Khannah calls YHWH 'YHWH of Hosts' — Tsvaot. This is one of the earliest uses of this title in the covenant literature. 'Hosts' refers to the heavenly armies under YHWH's command. Khannah, a barren woman in personal anguish, invokes the Commander of all cosmic forces in her private prayer. The title matters: she is not calling on a local deity or a household guardian. She is addressing the Creator of the universe for a personal, intimate need. The prayer's theological range — from personal grief to cosmic sovereignty — is deliberate. YHWH who commands armies is also YHWH who opens wombs. The prayer holds both without tension.

faq.question: What does Sha'ul hiding among the baggage reveal about his character?
faq.answer: At the moment of YHWH's public designation, Sha'ul hides. The lot falls on him, the people cannot find him, and YHWH must tell them where he is — hiding among the equipment. This beginning echoes how his story ends: a man chosen for greatness who consistently retreats at the decisive moment. His initial humility (he said earlier: 'Am I not a Benjaminite, from the smallest tribe?') turns into a repeated pattern of flight from accountability and responsibility. The same quality that makes him seem humble at the start becomes evasion and cowardice under pressure. The baggage hiding at Mitspah is the first marker of a character that never fully becomes what YHWH calls it to be.

faq.question: What does Eli's failure with his sons reveal about priestly covenant responsibility?
faq.answer: Eli knew what his sons were doing. He rebuked them. But he did not remove them. YHWH's judgment is specific: 'You honor your sons more than you honor me.' The covenant failure is not ignorance — it is prioritizing family loyalty over covenant fidelity. The same man who correctly identifies YHWH calling the child Shemu'el failed to manage his own house. The judgment against Eli's house (every male will die young, there will be no old man in his house) is severe precisely because his covenant responsibility was highest. The priest who stewards the meeting place between YHWH and Yisra'el bears the heaviest accountability for what that meeting place becomes.

faq.question: How did the Ark return from Philistine territory?
faq.answer: The Philistines were afflicted with plagues for seven months while the Ark was among them. Their priests designed a test: a new cart, two nursing cows that had never been yoked, with their calves shut away. If the cows went directly to Bet-Shemesh without returning to their calves, it was YHWH's hand. The cows went straight to Bet-Shemesh. The Ark returned on a Philistine cart, with golden guilt offerings for the plague (five golden tumors and five golden mice). What began as the capture of a defeated deity ended as the Ark's triumphant return, with the Philistines sending tribute. YHWH's reputation among the Philistines outlasted his people's unfaithfulness.

faq.question: What does the Ebenezer stone at Mitspah mark?
faq.answer: The stone Shemu'el sets up after the Philistine defeat marks a covenant turning point. 'Ebenezer' — the Stone of Help — was also the name of the place where the Ark was captured in 1 Shemu'el 4:1. By naming the new stone Ebenezer, Shemu'el reclaims the name from defeat: the same location that bore the memory of covenant failure now bears the memory of covenant restoration. 'Till now YHWH has helped us' means: from the beginning, through the wilderness, through the conquest, through the judges, through Eli's failure — YHWH has consistently been the helping stone. The monument is both backward-looking gratitude and forward-looking covenant claim.
